solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Old poet revitalised — one quiet for so long (6-3)

indicatorNotes.revitalised: given new life and remade, so the letters are rearranged into a fresh form

annotation.surface: An elderly poet, restored to vigour, says goodbye after a long silence.
annotation.walkthrough: TOODLE-PIP is dated British slang for goodbye. 'So long' looks like a length of time after 'quiet for', but it is the farewell.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by equivalent phrase: both are breezy farewells, the answer being dated upper-class British slang.

entries.clue: Chief villain so liable to be brought down? (3-5)

annotation.definition: so liable to be brought down?

blocks.note: top = chief, as in top dog
a heavy is the villain in a film or play

annotation.surface: A chief villain is so wicked he deserves to be toppled.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: the whole clue also describes a villain who is asking to be knocked over.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic, question-marked description: weight concentrated high up makes a thing unstable and easy to topple.

entries.clue: Regularly taking milk kept in cask (2,3)

blocks.note: if you are on a drug, you are regularly taking it
to milk or tap a source is to draw from it

annotation.surface: Someone habitually drinking milk stored in a barrel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' tempts you towards alternate letters, but no run of every other letter here spells anything useful; it belongs with 'taking' as ON.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: beer drawn straight from the barrel through a tap is said to be available this way.

entries.clue: One leaves peculiarly gelatinous lobster (9)

indicatorNotes.leaves: to leave is to go away, so the I departs from the word
indicatorNotes.peculiarly: in an odd, irregular way, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: GELATINOUS with its I removed; anagram fodder, 9 letters
one = I, the letter that leaves

annotation.surface: One diner walks away from an oddly jelly-like lobster.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' could be foliage, but here it is the verb: one letter walks out.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain translation: the French word names the spiny or rock lobster, a crustacean without big claws.

entries.clue: Fast train’s terminus in Lancashire location (7)

indicatorNotes.terminus: a terminus is the end of the line, so take the last letter of 'train'

blocks.note: presto is the musical marking for very fast

annotation.surface: An express train finishes its run somewhere in Lancashire.
annotation.walkthrough: Lancashire is a county in north-west England. The city is a major railway junction on the West Coast line, which suits the train surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this city is the county's administrative centre in north-west England.

entries.clue: First woman to criticise artist holding party (7)

indicatorNotes.holding: to hold something is to keep it in your grip, so PAN and RA grip DO between them

blocks.note: critics pan a show they dislike

annotation.surface: The first woman to criticise an artist does so while he is hosting a party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First woman to criticise' reads as a pioneering critic, but 'to' is only a link after the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Myth: Hesiod names her as the first mortal woman, fashioned by the gods, who opened the jar of evils.

entries.clue: Rose denied starter had a row (5)

indicatorNotes.denied starter: to be denied your starter is to lose the first course, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: SOARED (rose, as a bird does) without its first letter S

annotation.surface: A woman called Rose, refused a first course, had an argument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a name or a flower but is the past tense of rise; 'had a row' reads as a quarrel but means rowed a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb sense: to oar is an old word for to row, so the past tense means rowed, not quarrelled.

entries.clue: Ancient characters in hotel try rolls before noon (5)

indicatorNotes.rolls: something that rolls over turns end to end, so H and GO come out back to front

blocks.note: H = hotel in the NATO alphabet
have a go = have a try

annotation.surface: In a hotel, someone tries the bread rolls at breakfast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread, but it is a verb turning H GO over.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the early Irish alphabet of notches cut on stone edges, from around the fifth century.

entries.clue: Mad about one’s husband, very beautiful (9)

indicatorNotes.about: about in the sense of around: RAVING surrounds the other letters

blocks.note: one = I, and the 's is IS

annotation.surface: She is crazy about her husband, who is very handsome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mad about' reads as besotted, but 'about' is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: something that ravishes the senses is stunningly lovely.

entries.clue: Fill bowl with an accompaniment to coffee? (6)

indicatorNotes.Fill: to fill a bowl is to put something inside it, so AN goes into DISH

annotation.surface: An instruction to fill a bowl with something to have alongside coffee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'An' looks like part of the definition but is the filling.
annotation.definitionFit: Short for Danish pastry, the sweet flaky bun traditionally served with a cup of coffee.

entries.clue: Metal stanchion — piano leg contains it (5)

indicatorNotes.contains: to contain something is to have it inside, so P ON holds IT

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

annotation.surface: A metal support: the leg of a piano has one inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: Cricket calls the half of the field on the batsman's leg side the on side, so leg = ON.
annotation.definitionFit: Climbing term: the metal spike hammered into rock to anchor a rope acts as a small stanchion.

entries.clue: English kestrel, wingless, close to Vatican City (9)

indicatorNotes.wingless: a bird's wings are at its sides, so the word loses its outer letters
indicatorNotes.close to: the close of something is its end, so take the last letter of Vatican

blocks.note: WINDHOVER, a name for the kestrel, without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: An English kestrel with clipped wings ends up near the Vatican.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vatican City' reads as one place, but City is the definition on its own. Windhover is an old name for the kestrel, from its hovering; Hopkins wrote a poem of that title.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a Dutch city, home of Philips and PSV.

entries.clue: Apollo periodically seen in way out adventure (7)

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals, so take every other letter
indicatorNotes.seen in: to be seen in a place is to be inside it, so PLO sits within EXIT

blocks.note: an exit is a way out

annotation.surface: An Apollo mission, now and then spotted on a far-out adventure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Way out' reads as far-out, describing the adventure, but it is the container.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a daring deed or bold escapade.

entries.clue: Old Saxon prophet’s one for eastern assimilation (7)

indicatorNotes.one for eastern: X for Y means X stands in place of Y, so I (one) replaces E (eastern)

blocks.note: S = Saxon, the standard dictionary abbreviation
MOSES the prophet with its E changed to I

annotation.surface: An old Saxon prophet offers one of his own for the eastern world to absorb.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prophet's' ends in 's, so it reads as MOSES, and the swap works on those letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: gradual, unconscious absorption of ideas, taken from the chemistry of liquids passing a membrane.

entries.clue: World with a Giovanni perhaps is poetic creation (5,3,6)

blocks.note: Venus is a planet, a world
Don Giovanni, Mozart's opera hero; 'perhaps' marks him as one example of a don

annotation.surface: Don Giovanni, the great seducer, turned into a poem.
annotation.walkthrough: The seducer theme carries over: the poem is about the goddess of love pursuing a reluctant youth.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Shakespeare's 1593 narrative poem is a work of verse.

entries.clue: Chap, Athenian, ridiculously large (9)

indicatorNotes.ridiculously: in an absurd, disordered way, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A man from Athens who is absurdly big.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Large' looks like part of the joke about the Athenian's size, but it supplies the last letter of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Crossword convention: any man's given name can be clued as 'chap'.

entries.clue: Original note taken in second supplication? (3,6)

indicatorNotes.taken in: taken in as in admitted into a house, so UR FA goes inside OTHER

blocks.note: every second day = every other day
ur- is the prefix for original, as in Urtext
fa, the fourth note of the sol-fa scale

annotation.surface: An original note is taken into account in a second appeal.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark allows the Lord's Prayer, known by its opening words, to be called a supplication.
annotation.definitionFit: Name from the opening words of the Lord's Prayer, which is a petition to God.

entries.clue: Start describing my activities at restaurant? (8)

blocks.note: where I was: in it, the restaurant being 'it'
what I did there, told in the first person: I ate

annotation.surface: Someone begins an account of what they did at a restaurant.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a whole sentence someone might say about a restaurant, 'In it, I ate', run together into one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym as a verb: to set something going or begin it.

entries.clue: King united there with knight and monster seizing power (5,9)

indicatorNotes.seizing: to seize something is to grab hold of it, so the string takes P inside

blocks.note: U = united, as in football team names

annotation.surface: A king unites his lands with the help of a knight while a monster grabs power.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is pure Arthurian legend, and 'pendragon' itself means chief dragon. P lands inside THERE, not inside the monster.
annotation.definitionFit: Legend: Arthur's father, who reigned over Britain in the Arthurian tales.

entries.clue: Animal run following trail around north east (7)

indicatorNotes.around: around in the sense of surrounding: PATH wraps round N
indicatorNotes.following: following means coming after, so R goes at the end

blocks.note: R = run, as on cricket scorecards

annotation.surface: An animal on the run follows a trail through the north-east.
annotation.walkthrough: 'North east' reads as one region, but only north goes inside PATH; east follows it.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a big cat, usually a black leopard.

entries.clue: New look for Welsh entertainer (7)

annotation.surface: A Welsh performer gets a makeover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New look' reads as a makeover, but it splits into two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Ivor Novello, the Cardiff-born composer and matinee idol.

entries.clue: Press worker in mechanical repetition packing papers up (6)

indicatorNotes.packing: a case packing something holds it inside, so ROTE holds ID
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters turn round

blocks.note: learning by rote is mechanical repetition

annotation.surface: A printing-press worker, doing the same task over and over, packs up the papers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Press' suggests a machine, fitting the mechanical surface, but here it is the press as in newspapers.
annotation.definitionFit: The press means journalism, and the person in charge of a newspaper's content works in it.

entries.clue: Mostly maddened, recycled empty bottles (4,3)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.recycled: recycled material is broken down and remade, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: MADDENED without its last letter; anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Someone half-crazed takes the empties to the recycling bank.
annotation.walkthrough: The recycling surface fits the empties perfectly, which hides that 'recycled' is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: drained bottles left after a drinking session.

entries.clue: In sea abroad this writer’s one playing dumb (5)

indicatorNotes.In: in means inside, so IM goes within MER

blocks.note: this writer = I, the setter; this writer's = I'm

annotation.surface: Out at sea overseas, the setter confesses to being a silent performer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One playing dumb' sounds like someone feigning ignorance; here it is literal, a performer who acts without speaking.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Dumb' in its old sense of silent: a mime artist performs without speaking.

entries.clue: Struggler submerged we hear in river crossing? (7)

indicatorNotes.we hear: what we hear is the sound of the words, so the answer sounds like them

blocks.note: a vier is one who vies, a struggler

annotation.surface: Someone struggling in a river goes under.
annotation.walkthrough: The drowning swimmer is the misdirection; the words are only there for their sound.
annotation.definitionFit: Question-marked extension: this long arched bridge more usually spans a valley but can carry traffic over water.

entries.clue: Something nasty afoot with British deserting alliance (5)

indicatorNotes.deserting: a deserter abandons his post, so B leaves the word

blocks.note: a bunion is a painful swelling on the foot
B = British, the letter that deserts

annotation.surface: Something sinister is going on as the British walk out of an alliance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Something nasty afoot' reads as a plot brewing, but 'afoot' is literal: on the foot.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a joining together of parties or states.

entries.clue: Victorious pilot holding uniform speed? (9)

indicatorNotes.holding: to hold something is to keep it inside, so TRIAL keeps U MPH within

blocks.note: a pilot scheme is a trial
U = uniform in the NATO alphabet
mph, miles per hour, measures speed

annotation.surface: A winning pilot keeps a steady speed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' paints an airman and 'uniform speed' a steady pace, but pilot means a test run and uniform is just U.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: marking or celebrating a win, as in a triumphal arch.

entries.clue: City integral to Bahai faith (5)

indicatorNotes.integral to: forming an inseparable part of, so the answer lies inside the words

annotation.surface: A city central to the Bahai religion.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is true: the city holds the Bahai World Centre and the Shrine of the Bab.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an Israeli port on Mount Carmel.

entries.clue: Governor having regret about left — and right (5)

indicatorNotes.about: about in the sense of around: RUE surrounds L

annotation.surface: A political leader regrets the left and the right alike.
annotation.walkthrough: The political surface of left and right hides two single letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: one who holds power over a state.

entries.clue: One cutting wild or garden flower (3,6)

indicatorNotes.cutting: to cut into something is to go inside it, so I enters the rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.wild: untamed and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone cutting flowers, wild or from the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: The gardening surface makes 'flower' a bloom, but it is read as flow-er, something that flows.
annotation.definitionFit: Crossword convention: a 'flower' is something that flows, a river, here the one along the Texas-Mexico border.
